significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would establish that the "degree to which a learned feature, steering vector, or circuit transfers" follows a monotone typological-distance law, with semantic and syntactic components governed by different distance dimensions; this is form (iii), fixing expected transfer orderings and explanatory variables for language pairs not yet examined. It establishes both a behavioral phenomenon—systematic transfer degradation—and a mechanistic regularity about causal feature and circuit reuse, although not the deeper cause of that regularity; this matters because Pires et al. (ACL 2019) and Lauscher et al. (EMNLP 2020) use linguistic similarity to explain task-level transfer, making it consequential to know whether the same predictor governs reusable internals. The branches are determinate: confirmation supports the monotonic law and component-type dissociation, while refutation rules out typological distance as the governing predictor of internal-component transfer rather than merely reporting a missing component. Topic substitution fails: the generic question of language-independent versus language-specific mechanisms would not itself earn this score; the extra weight comes specifically from the claimed monotonic relation and axis-specific dissociation.

reach.justification: The concrete handles are the "per-component transfer score (target-language causal effect / source effect)" and the component-specific attribution to typological sub-distances, which together can forecast which source-language features or circuits will transfer poorly. This is potentially ex ante because typological distances are available before transferring or deploying a component, leaving model builders an action window for language-specific training, auditing, or intervention. After components are re-extracted on another model, the conclusion still predicts an ordering—greater relevant distance means lower transfer—and which distance dimension should dominate, so more than a search procedure survives recalibration; however, no invariance across architectures, scales, or training recipes is expressly claimed, which limits the scope below the top band. Topic substitution again fails: the broad multilingual-representation topic supplies no such predictor, whereas this claim specifically hands multilingual-model researchers and deployment auditors a distance-based screening rule, though it does not directly travel outside AI.
